title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 17–18
description: Advanced vocabulary for workplace attire, styles and fashion trends, clothing metaphors, accommodation types and idioms relating to home and lifestyles.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided Cambridge textbook to select targets. Brazilian Portuguese translations, English usage notes and all example sentences are newly written rather than copied from the textbook.

audit.scope: Unit 17 sections A–D and Language help, exercises 17.1–17.5; Unit 18 sections A–C and exercises 18.1–18.4; and the corresponding answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied where reliable, mostly for individual words. Empty IPA for longer expressions avoids conjectural connected-speech transcriptions. US/UK differences are noted as appropriate.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing content is in English except for Brazilian Portuguese in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Read the four source teaching and exercise pages (PDF 42–45) and relevant answer-key pages (PDF 222–223), including the Language help box. Authored examples and notes independently. Performed programmatic schema parity, item ID uniqueness across available Advanced workstream files, required-field and speech-target checks. Browser TTS and actual import were not tested.
audit.limitations: The package contains no MP3 assets. Browser import, Word/Sentence TTS and speech recognition remain untested. Cultural terms such as High Street, council housing and granny flat follow predominantly British usage; regional meanings and actual dress requirements vary.

units.title: Unit 17 — All the rage: clothes and fashion
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 40–41 (PDF pages 42–43).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Leisure and lifestyle · clothing, appearance, fashion and figurative language
learningObjectives: Use workplace dress vocabulary accurately and choose natural terms for clothing fit, fabrics and accessories.
Distinguish British and American shopping expressions and describe styles without confusing connotations.
Describe trends with idioms such as all the rage, on trend and catch on.
Understand metaphors involving clothing, financial constraints, secrecy and achievement.

sectionsChecked: A · Dressing for work and Language help
B · Words and expressions about clothes

items.pt: desleixado; malvestido
items.example: He turned up to the awards ceremony looking rather scruffy.
items.note: Describes an untidy appearance or clothes; generally critical and informal.

items.pt: pessoa mal-arrumada ou desleixada
items.example: His friends teased him for being a scruff at formal events.
items.note: Informal noun for a person who dresses untidily; scruffy is the adjective.

items.pt: código de vestimenta; regras sobre como se vestir
items.example: The laboratory has a dress code for visitors entering restricted areas.
items.note: A social or institutional rule about suitable clothing; dress code is usually countable.

items.pt: traje profissional; vestimenta para o trabalho
items.example: Business attire is expected at meetings with external clients.
items.note: Attire is a relatively formal uncountable noun for clothing.

items.pt: imagem profissional
items.example: A carefully chosen outfit can help project a professional image.
items.note: Project an image means present a particular impression to other people.

items.pt: mostrar; deixar à mostra; revelar
items.example: The neckline revealed more skin than the company policy allowed.
items.note: In a clothing context, reveal means show or expose; elsewhere it can mean disclose information.

items.pt: decote entre os seios; sulco entre os seios
items.example: The costume had a low neckline that revealed cleavage.
items.note: Refers to the space or visible line between the breasts; can also have technical meanings.

items.pt: parte da barriga entre o peito e a cintura
items.example: The cropped top left her midriff uncovered.
items.note: Part of the body, particularly the abdomen between chest and waist.

items.pt: tecido transparente; tecido que deixa ver através
items.example: The costume designer used a see-through fabric over a lining.
items.note: See-through describes material through which the body or other layers remain visible.

items.pt: cafona; antiquado e sem estilo
items.example: She rejected the frumpy jacket in favour of a modern blazer.
items.note: Negative adjective for unfashionable, rather dull clothes; potentially unkind if applied to a person.

items.pt: conjunto de roupas; look
items.example: He chose a comfortable outfit for the conference dinner.
items.note: A set of clothes worn together, usually for a particular occasion.

items.pt: terno; conjunto social
items.example: He wore a dark suit to the interview.
items.note: As a noun, a suit is a coordinated set such as a jacket and trousers; compare suit as a verb.

items.pt: extremamente útil; de valor inestimável
items.example: Reliable safety boots are invaluable during maintenance work.
items.note: Means extremely useful or valuable, not worthless; contrast valueless.

items.pt: sem valor; sem utilidade ou valor material
items.example: The counterfeit tickets were completely valueless.
items.note: Valueless is an opposite of valuable; invaluable is not.

items.pt: acessórios de vestuário
items.example: She kept her accessories discreet for the formal presentation.
items.note: Plural of accessory; clothing extras such as belts, shoes and jewellery.

items.pt: abotoaduras
items.example: He received silver cufflinks as a graduation gift.
items.note: Decorative fasteners for the cuffs of certain dress shirts, usually used in pairs.

items.pt: dia de trabalho com vestimenta mais informal
items.example: Our office has a dress-down day on the last Friday of each month.
items.note: An occasion at work when less formal clothing is permitted.

items.pt: uniforme
items.example: The airline introduced a new uniform for cabin staff.
items.note: Standardised clothing worn by members of an organisation or occupation.

items.pt: roupas de proteção; vestimenta de segurança
items.example: Protective clothing is compulsory when handling the chemicals.
items.note: Functional clothes worn to reduce workplace hazards; clothing is uncountable.

items.pt: macacão de trabalho; roupa de proteção integral
items.example: The technicians put on overalls before cleaning the machinery.
items.note: British English plural noun for work clothes covering most of the body; related US terms vary.

items.pt: capacete de segurança
items.example: A safety helmet is required throughout the construction site.
items.note: Helmet designed to protect the head; hard hat is common for industrial construction helmets.

items.pt: revelador; que deixa muita pele à mostra
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: She chose a less revealing dress for the formal reception.
items.note: Revealing clothing exposes a relatively large amount of skin; avoid confusing with the figurative meaning revealing information.

items.pt: curto e com pouco tecido; sumário
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: He thought the skimpy costume was unsuitable for the cold weather.
items.note: Usually describes clothing made from little material; often carries a disapproving tone.

items.pt: largo; folgado
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: She prefers baggy trousers when travelling.
items.note: Describes loose-fitting clothes, contrasting with tight or clingy.

items.pt: justo; colado ao corpo
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: The fabric became clingy in humid weather.
items.note: Clingy clothes fit closely to the body; a clingy person is emotionally overdependent.

items.pt: chique; elegante; sofisticado
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: The hotel lobby was decorated in a chic, understated style.
items.note: Pronounced /ʃiːk/; describes fashionable elegance rather than extravagance.

items.pt: esporte fino; casual elegante
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: The invitation requested smart-casual dress rather than formal evening wear.
items.note: Smart-casual combines neat, stylish clothes with a less formal look.

items.pt: se produzir; se arrumar muito para sair
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: They got dolled up for the end-of-year party.
items.note: Informal phrase for dressing up attractively; may suggest more elaborate grooming.

items.pt: se arrumar com roupa elegante; vestir-se para uma ocasião
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: We got dressed up for the charity ball.
items.note: Can mean put on smart or formal clothing rather than simply get dressed.

items.pt: todo produzido; vestido com extrema elegância
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: They arrived done up to the nines for the opening night.
items.note: Informal idiom for being very smartly or elaborately dressed.

items.pt: roupas de grife; roupas de estilista
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: She saves money by buying second-hand designer clothes.
items.note: Clothing produced or marketed under a recognised fashion-designer label.

items.pt: grife; etiqueta de marca de estilista
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: The coat had a designer label but a remarkably plain cut.
items.note: Describes an identifiable fashion brand; designer-label clothes is a common attributive phrase.

items.pt: rua comercial principal; comércio de lojas comuns
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: He bought his work clothes on the High Street rather than from luxury boutiques.
items.note: British term for ordinary central shopping streets and mainstream retailers; its meaning is cultural, not a particular street.

items.pt: sob medida; feito conforme as medidas da pessoa
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: She ordered a made-to-measure jacket for the ceremony.
items.note: Custom-sized clothing; not necessarily fully bespoke tailoring.

items.pt: pronto para vestir; comprado pronto na loja
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: His wedding suit was bought off the peg.
items.note: British idiom for ready-made clothes; US English often says off the rack.

items.pt: pronto para vestir; comprado pronto na loja
items.section: B · Words and expressions about clothes
items.example: She found a well-fitting coat off the rack.
items.note: Common American-English equivalent of British off the peg.

items.pt: a última moda; muito em alta
items.example: Vintage trainers are all the rage among local designers.
items.note: Idiomatic expression meaning extremely fashionable or popular at a particular time.

items.pt: a moda mais recente; a última tendência
items.example: The boutique specialises in the very latest fashion.
items.note: Very strengthens latest; a term for what is most fashionable now.

items.pt: o auge da moda; o que há de mais moderno
items.example: Wide-brimmed hats were the height of fashion that season.
items.note: Idiomatic superlative for something exceptionally fashionable.

items.pt: atualizadíssimo; com as novidades mais recentes
items.example: The magazine publishes up-to-the-minute style reports.
items.note: Compound adjective normally placed before a noun.

items.pt: lançar uma nova tendência
items.example: The young designer set a new trend with recycled fabrics.
items.note: Set a trend means initiate a fashion or new pattern of behaviour.

items.pt: lançador de tendências; pessoa que dita moda
items.example: The musician became a trend-setter among younger fans.
items.note: A person whose choices influence what others wear or do.

items.pt: na moda; em alta
items.example: Loose-fitting linen shirts are on trend this summer.
items.note: In fashion; especially frequent in retail and lifestyle writing.

items.pt: item indispensável da moda; objeto de desejo
items.example: The compact handbag was advertised as the season’s must-have item.
items.note: Marketing-influenced expression for a fashionable product many people want.

items.pt: pegar; cair no gosto popular; tornar-se popular
items.example: The idea initially seemed odd, but it soon caught on.
items.note: Intransitive phrasal verb: a fashion or idea catches on; past tense caught on.

items.pt: escravo da moda; pessoa excessivamente influenciada por tendências
items.example: He refuses to become a slave to fashion and wears what feels comfortable.
items.note: Usually disapproving; suggests following trends without independent judgement.

items.pt: ficar bem em você; combinar com você
items.example: That shade of green really suits you.
items.note: Of clothing or colour, suit means look good on a person; not the noun a suit.

items.pt: falar de improviso; falar sem preparação
items.example: She spoke off the cuff when the moderator unexpectedly invited her to comment.
items.note: An idiom for speaking without prepared notes or a rehearsed text.

items.pt: ter ligação muito próxima com; agir em conluio com
items.example: The supplier was accused of being hand in glove with the purchasing manager.
items.note: Suggests a very close association, sometimes suspicious or improper; followed by with.
items.speechText: be hand in glove with the boss

items.pt: com pouquíssimo dinheiro; com orçamento apertado
items.example: They developed the prototype on a shoestring.
items.note: Means with very little money; run, live or operate on a shoestring.

items.pt: sem luxos; básico; sem extras
items.example: The company chose a no-frills venue for its annual meeting.
items.note: Means stripped of unnecessary extras, often to lower costs; hyphenated before a noun.

items.word: put the team in a straitjacket
items.pt: limitar excessivamente a autonomia da equipe
items.example: The rigid rules put the team in a straitjacket.
items.note: Metaphorical pattern put someone in a straitjacket = severely restrict their freedom.

items.word: draw a veil over the matter
items.pt: deixar o assunto de lado; não tocar no assunto
items.example: The committee decided to draw a veil over the matter after reaching an agreement.
items.note: Idiom draw a veil over something = avoid further discussion of an unpleasant subject.

items.word: have a plan up your sleeve
items.pt: ter um plano guardado na manga
items.example: I suspect our director has a plan up her sleeve.
items.note: Idiom have something up your sleeve: keep a secret idea or tactic in reserve.

items.pt: apertar o cinto; cortar gastos
items.example: After moving to a smaller budget, the team had to tighten its belt.
items.note: Metaphor for reducing spending; the possessive changes with the subject.

items.pt: ficar encurralado; ter os movimentos restringidos
items.example: The spectators were hemmed in by barriers and could not leave quickly.
items.note: Literally related to sewing a hem; figuratively means being surrounded or constrained.

items.pt: lotado; abarrotado; prestes a estourar de tão cheio
items.example: The small conference room was bursting at the seams.
items.note: Metaphor drawn from sewn seams that split under pressure; means extremely full.

items.pt: envolto em segredo; mantido em sigilo
items.example: The negotiations were cloaked in secrecy until the deal was signed.
items.note: Metaphor from cloak as a covering; often used in reporting secretive processes.

items.pt: motivo de orgulho; conquista importante
items.example: Winning the research award was a feather in her cap.
items.note: An achievement that brings personal credit or pride.

units.title: Unit 18 — Home styles, lifestyles
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 42–43 (PDF pages 44–45).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Leisure and lifestyle · housing and figurative expressions relating to home and life
learningObjectives: Distinguish rented, furnished, social and other forms of housing in predominantly British English.
Use idioms involving home and house for relationships, reputation and uncomfortable truths.
Apply figurative life expressions to risk, excitement, renewal and seriousness.
Recognise additional home and life expressions introduced by the exercises.

sectionsChecked: A · Home styles and housing vocabulary
B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life

items.pt: imóvel ocupado sem autorização do proprietário
items.example: The council inspected a disused warehouse that had become a squat.
items.note: A building occupied without the owner’s permission; squat can also be a verb with related meaning.

items.pt: ocupante irregular de imóvel
items.example: The documentary interviewed a squatter living in an abandoned factory.
items.note: A person occupying a property without the owner’s permission; distinct from an ordinary tenant.

items.pt: casebre; moradia muito precária
items.example: The abandoned cottage had become a damp, unsafe hovel.
items.note: A very small, dirty or badly maintained home; sharply negative.

items.pt: deteriorado; malconservado
items.example: They restored a run-down terrace house near the station.
items.note: Describes buildings or areas in poor condition; can also describe an exhausted person.

items.pt: moradia alugada; imóvel alugado
items.example: Rented accommodation was difficult to find near the university.
items.note: Accommodation is generally uncountable in British English.

items.pt: moradia mobiliada
items.example: Furnished accommodation costs more but saves the expense of buying furniture.
items.note: Comes with furniture; furnished and unfurnished are the relevant alternatives.

items.pt: moradia sem mobília
items.example: They opted for unfurnished accommodation because they owned their furniture.
items.note: A rented home without furniture; arrangements for appliances may vary.

items.pt: cobertura de luxo
items.example: The penthouse overlooked the river and the city skyline.
items.note: A high-end flat at or near the top of a building.

items.pt: habitação pública municipal; moradia social administrada pelo poder público
items.example: Council housing has a distinctive historical role in the United Kingdom.
items.note: British term referring to housing provided by local authorities; categories differ internationally.

items.pt: habitação social; moradia subsidiada
items.example: The city approved new social housing near the railway station.
items.note: Broad term for supported affordable accommodation, often with income-related eligibility.

items.pt: conjunto habitacional público municipal
items.example: The council estate underwent a major renovation programme.
items.note: British English: development containing council-owned housing; avoid using the term as a judgement of residents.

items.pt: apartamentos em edifícios altos
items.example: The proposal includes high-rise flats alongside community facilities.
items.note: High-rise refers to tall buildings with many floors; flat is the usual British term for apartment.

items.pt: edifício residencial alto; torre de apartamentos
items.example: The old tower block was refurbished to improve insulation.
items.note: British noun for a tall building divided into many flats or offices.

items.pt: edícula ou apartamento anexo para parente idoso
items.example: They built a granny flat so her father could live nearby with privacy.
items.note: Informal British term for a self-contained annexe associated with a larger family home.

items.word: get on like a house on fire
items.pt: dar-se extremamente bem com alguém
items.section: B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
items.example: The new colleagues got on like a house on fire from their first meeting.
items.note: British idiom for quickly developing a warm and lively relationship.

items.pt: nome conhecido por todos; celebridade ou marca muito conhecida
items.section: B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
items.example: The scientist became a household name after the televised lectures.
items.note: A person or brand known by the general public, not merely a person known within one household.

items.pt: nome ou expressão de conhecimento geral
items.section: B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
items.example: The phrase soon became a household word across the country.
items.note: A widely known expression or name; similar to household name, although the latter is more common.

items.pt: por conta da casa; oferecido gratuitamente pelo estabelecimento
items.section: B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
items.example: The manager gave us dessert on the house after the delay.
items.note: Typically used by bars, hotels and restaurants when something is free to the customer.

items.pt: verdades duras de ouvir; verdades incômodas
items.section: B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
items.example: Her mentor offered some home truths about her management style.
items.note: Unpleasant but accurate observations, often offered as criticism or frank advice.

items.pt: nada de especial; nada extraordinário
items.section: B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
items.example: The meal was acceptable but nothing to write home about.
items.note: Understated idiom for something ordinary or unimpressive.

items.pt: cair a ficha; ser plenamente compreendido; afetar profundamente
items.section: B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
items.example: The seriousness of the funding shortfall finally hit home.
items.note: A fact or emotion hits home when its significance becomes clear or strongly felt.

items.pt: fique à vontade; sinta-se em casa
items.section: B · Idioms and expressions relating to house and home
items.example: Please make yourself at home while I finish preparing lunch.
items.note: Friendly invitation to feel relaxed as a guest; yourself changes with number.

items.pt: vida agitada e cheia de emoção
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: After years of life in the fast lane, she moved to a quiet village.
items.note: A lifestyle involving high activity, excitement and sometimes risk.

items.word: have the time of your life
items.pt: divertir-se muito; passar momentos inesquecíveis
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: The children had the time of their lives at the science festival.
items.note: Strong idiom for having an exceptionally enjoyable experience.

items.word: get a new lease of life
items.pt: ganhar novo ânimo; ganhar uma nova vida
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: The old theatre got a new lease of life after the restoration.
items.note: Applied to people or things becoming energetic, active or useful again.

items.pt: vida muito dura; vida de sofrimento
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: He described his first years at sea as a dog’s life.
items.note: Usually describes a difficult or unhappy existence; this fixed idiom need not describe dogs.

items.pt: levar uma vida protegida, afastada de dificuldades
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: She had led a sheltered life before moving abroad on her own.
items.note: Someone protected from many dangers or difficulties, sometimes lacking experience.

items.word: a matter of life and death
items.pt: questão de vida ou morte; assunto gravíssimo
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: For the rescue team, rapid communication was a matter of life and death.
items.note: Refers to something of the utmost importance or literally critical to survival.

items.word: not a matter of life and death
items.pt: não é caso de vida ou morte; não é tão grave
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: Missing one train is inconvenient but not a matter of life and death.
items.note: Conventional negative variant that plays down the seriousness of a situation.

items.word: take your life in your hands
items.pt: colocar a própria vida em risco
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: You take your life in your hands when you ignore the marked trail in a storm.
items.note: Strong idiom for voluntarily doing something very dangerous.

items.pt: dar novo fôlego a; revitalizar
items.section: C · Idioms and metaphors relating to life
items.example: The new director breathed new life into the neglected programme.
items.note: Bring renewed energy, ideas or vitality to a project or organisation.
items.speechText: breathe new life into the project

items.pt: tirar a própria vida; morrer por suicídio
items.section: Exercise 18.4 · Further home and life idioms
items.example: The public-health campaign explains how to support people who may be at risk of taking their own lives.
items.note: Euphemistic expression for dying by suicide; discuss the topic sensitively and avoid euphemisms that obscure meaning in clinical contexts.

items.pt: levar a plateia ao delírio; arrancar aplausos entusiasmados
items.section: Exercise 18.4 · Further home and life idioms
items.example: The comedian brought the house down with her final routine.
items.note: Here house means an audience, not a building; the idiom expresses an enthusiastic response.

items.pt: de todas as camadas sociais; de diferentes origens e profissões
items.section: Exercise 18.4 · Further home and life idioms
items.example: The public lecture attracted people from all walks of life.
items.note: Means from many social groups, occupations and backgrounds.

items.pt: castelo de cartas; estrutura frágil prestes a desmoronar
items.section: Exercise 18.4 · Further home and life idioms
items.example: The financial arrangement proved to be a house of cards.
items.note: A weak or unstable system that can collapse after a small disturbance.

items.word: eat you out of house and home
items.pt: comer tanto que quase deixa alguém sem comida
items.section: Exercise 18.4 · Further home and life idioms
items.example: The visiting teenagers nearly ate us out of house and home.
items.note: Humorous exaggeration about guests consuming a very large amount of food.

items.word: the life and soul of the party
items.pt: a alma da festa; a pessoa que anima a reunião
items.section: Exercise 18.4 · Further home and life idioms
items.example: No one was surprised when Lena became the life and soul of the party.
items.note: British idiom for an energetic, sociable person who makes a gathering enjoyable.

items.pt: ser despejado; ser retirado de um imóvel
items.section: Exercise 18.4 · Further home and life idioms
items.example: The tenants sought advice after being told they might be evicted.
items.note: Passive of evict, legally require someone to leave a property; source exercise mentions potential eviction.
